doc.title: Michael Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 22, 2021

title: Where compositions' titles come from
summary: Titles come last, after the music is finished; composing mood is not the mood you are in.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I’m not who makes too much out of titles and their relationship to the actual music but it seemed an effective way to start that piece because it left a lot of room for where to go with it.
Where do your titles come from?

Well they come last. You know sometimes I joke about you know the fan that comes up to you after the set and says, “Boy it must be so great to make music. When you’re feeling sad, do you want to write a sad song?” It’s like, “No, when I’m sad I want to watch — veg out in front of the television and crack open a beer” or, you know, the mood that you’re in is not what you’re in when you compose. You know? When you compose you’re in a certain frame of mind and you draw on your experience of various emotions and things that you want to communicate. You don’t necessarily have to be in that frame of mind when you are composing, obviously. So to answer the question, the last thing I think about usually is the title. It’s purely a musical experience or expression. It’s after that is complete then you can go back and say okay well what does this, what’s the mood of this piece? What does it evoke? What does it make you think of when you listen to it? And that’s when you start to think about a title. That’s when I start to think about a title.
